sections.label: Reading
sections.title: The Display Deadline
sections.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
This is a fictional school problem. Four students must finish a history display by Friday. They have one lunch meeting left and cannot stay after school. Their first plan used a large printed map, but the print shop has told them that it will not be ready until Monday. They have paper, markers and their research notes. Their teacher says accuracy and clear explanations matter more than expensive materials.

Jon suggests drawing the map by hand. This would keep the original design, but the group is worried that drawing details will take most of the meeting. A simpler map would still show the three places mentioned in their research.

Asha proposes replacing the map with three labeled information panels. Each panel would explain one place and include a small location sketch. Everyone could complete a panel or check the facts. However, visitors might find it harder to see the relationship between the places.

The group agrees to compare time, clarity and fair participation. They have not yet made a final decision. Before choosing, they need to estimate the work and identify a way to reduce each plan’s main weakness. They cannot solve the deadline problem simply by spending more money.

items.prompt: Why is the original plan no longer feasible?
What matters most to the teacher?
What is a drawback of the panels?
Has the group chosen its final solution?

sections.teacherNotes:
Teacher transcript:
Our group has a problem with tomorrow’s class presentation. We planned to meet in the music room after lunch, but another class is using it. We still need to practice together, and we cannot stay after school. There are four people in our group, and one of them needs a quiet place to hear the lines clearly.

One suggestion is to practice in the yard. There is plenty of space, but it can be noisy. Another suggestion is to use an empty classroom for fifteen minutes during lunch. That would be quieter, although our rehearsal time would be shorter. We would need to ask the teacher before using the room.

I initially preferred the yard because we could start immediately. After listening to the others, I changed my mind. A rehearsal is not useful if one person cannot follow it. We agreed to ask for the classroom and practice only the opening and the two most difficult transitions.

If the room is not available, our backup is to read the lines quietly in pairs and meet for five minutes to check the transitions. That is not ideal, but it gives everyone a role. Our decision puts clear communication ahead of having the longest possible rehearsal.

Read the questions aloud for young learners. Replay or reread in short sections if needed.

Jon suggests drawing the map by hand. This would keep the original design, but the group is worried that drawing details will take most of the meeting. A simpler map would still show the three places mentioned in their research.

Asha proposes replacing the map with three labeled information panels. Each panel would explain one place and include a small location sketch. Everyone could complete a panel or check the facts. However, visitors might find it harder to see the relationship between the places.

The group agrees to compare time, clarity and fair participation. They have not yet made a final decision. Before choosing, they need to estimate the work and identify a way to reduce each plan’s main weakness. They cannot solve the deadline problem simply by spending more money.

value.title: A Different Way to Rehearse
value.purpose: Describe a practical problem, evaluate two solutions against explicit criteria, and justify a group decision while acknowledging a drawback.
value.instructions: Listen once for the situation and again for details.
value.script:
Our group has a problem with tomorrow’s class presentation. We planned to meet in the music room after lunch, but another class is using it. We still need to practice together, and we cannot stay after school. There are four people in our group, and one of them needs a quiet place to hear the lines clearly.

One suggestion is to practice in the yard. There is plenty of space, but it can be noisy. Another suggestion is to use an empty classroom for fifteen minutes during lunch. That would be quieter, although our rehearsal time would be shorter. We would need to ask the teacher before using the room.

I initially preferred the yard because we could start immediately. After listening to the others, I changed my mind. A rehearsal is not useful if one person cannot follow it. We agreed to ask for the classroom and practice only the opening and the two most difficult transitions.

If the room is not available, our backup is to read the lines quietly in pairs and meet for five minutes to check the transitions. That is not ideal, but it gives everyone a role. Our decision puts clear communication ahead of having the longest possible rehearsal.
